title: Part 1, Chapter 6
paragraphs: About the diverting and important inquiry which the curate and the barber made into the library of our ingenious gentleman

He was still asleep, so the curate asked the niece for the keys of the room where the books — the source of all the mischief — were kept, and she gave them up very willingly. They all went in, the housekeeper with them, and found more than a hundred large volumes very well bound, and a number of smaller ones. The moment the housekeeper saw them she turned about and ran out of the room, then came back at once with a saucer of holy water and a sprinkler, saying, "Here, your worship, señor licentiate, sprinkle this room; don't leave any magician of the many there are in these books here to bewitch us in revenge for our plan to banish them from the world."

The housekeeper's simplicity made the licentiate laugh, and he directed the barber to hand him the books one by one, to see what they were about, since some might turn out not to deserve the penalty of fire.

"No," said the niece, "there is no reason to show mercy to any of them; they have all done damage; better fling them out of the window into the courtyard and pile them up and set fire to them; or take them out to the back yard, where the bonfire can be made without the smoke bothering anyone." The housekeeper said the same — they were both that eager for the slaughter of those innocents — but the curate would not agree without first reading at least the titles.

The first that Master Nicholas put into his hands was "The four books of Amadis of Gaul." "This seems a portentous thing," said the curate, "for, as I have heard, this was the first book of chivalry printed in Spain, and from it all the others derive their origin and birth; so it seems to me we should condemn it without appeal to the flames, as the founder of so vile a sect."
"No, sir," said the barber, "I too have heard that this is the best of all the books of this kind that have ever been written, and so, being uniquely fine of its kind, it should be pardoned."
"True," said the curate; "and for that reason let its life be spared for the present. Let's see this other one next to it."
"That," said the barber, "is the 'Sergas de Esplandian,' the lawful son of Amadis of Gaul."

"Then, truly," said the curate, "the father's merit should not be credited to the son. Take it, mistress housekeeper; open the window and fling it into the yard, and lay the foundation of the pile for the bonfire we're going to make."
The housekeeper obeyed with great satisfaction, and the worthy "Esplandian" went flying out into the yard to await with all patience the fire that was in store for him.
"Carry on," said the curate.
"This next one," said the barber, "is 'Amadis of Greece' — and indeed I think all of those on this side are of the same Amadis lineage."

"Then out into the yard with the whole lot of them," said the curate. "To have the burning of Queen Pintiquiniestra, and the shepherd Darinel with his eclogues, and the author's bedevilled and twisted discourses, I would burn the father who begot me along with them if he were going about in the guise of a knight-errant."
"I'm of the same mind," said the barber.
"And so am I," added the niece.
"In that case," said the housekeeper, "here — out into the yard with them!"
They were handed to her, and as there were a lot of them, she spared herself the staircase and flung them down out of the window.
"Who is that fat tub there?" said the curate.
"That," said the barber, "is 'Don Olivante de Laura.'"

"The author of that book," said the curate, "was the same who wrote 'The Garden of Flowers,' and truly there is no deciding which of the two books is the more truthful — or, to put it better, the less lying; all I can say is, send this one into the yard for a swaggering fool."
"This next is 'Florismarte of Hircania,'" said the barber.

"Señor Florismarte here?" said the curate. "Then by my faith he must take up his quarters in the yard, in spite of his marvellous birth and visionary adventures, for the stiffness and dryness of his style deserve nothing else. Out into the yard with him and the other, mistress housekeeper."
"With all my heart, señor," said she, and carried out the order with great delight.
"This," said the barber, "is 'The Knight Platir.'"
"An old book that," said the curate, "but I find no reason for mercy in it; send it after the others without appeal" — which was done.
Another book was opened, and they saw it was titled "The Knight of the Cross."
"For the sake of the holy name this book bears," said the curate, "its ignorance might be excused; but then, they say, 'behind the cross there's the devil' — to the fire with it."
Taking down another book, the barber said, "This is 'The Mirror of Chivalry.'"

"I know his worship," said the curate; "that's where Señor Reinaldos of Montalvan figures with his friends and comrades, greater thieves than Cacus, and the Twelve Peers of France with the veracious historian Turpin. As for them, I'm not for condemning them to more than perpetual banishment, because, at any rate, they have some share in the invention of the famous Matteo Boiardo, from which too the Christian poet Ludovico Ariosto wove his web — and as for him, if I find him here speaking any language but his own, I'll show him no respect whatever; but if he speaks his own tongue, I'll set him on my head."
"Well, I have him in Italian," said the barber, "but I don't understand him."

"Nor would it be a good thing if you did," said the curate; "and on that score we might have excused the Captain too, if he hadn't brought him into Spain and turned him into Castilian. He robbed him of a great deal of his natural force, as do all those who try to render books written in verse into another language: with all their care and cleverness, they can never come up to the originals as first produced. In short, I say that this book — and every other that turns up dealing with those French affairs — should be thrown into, or stored in, some dry well, until after more thought it is settled what to do with them. Always excepting one 'Bernardo del Carpio' that is going about, and another called 'Roncesvalles'; for these, if they come into my hands, shall pass straight into the housekeeper's, and from hers into the fire without reprieve."

To all this the barber gave his assent, and looked on it as right and proper, being convinced that the curate was so staunch a Catholic and loyal to the Truth that he would not for the world say anything against them. Opening another book, he saw it was "Palmerin de Oliva," and beside it was another called "Palmerin of England," at which the licentiate said, "Let the Olive be made firewood of at once and burnt until not even ashes are left; and let that Palm of England be kept and preserved as a thing unique. Let such another case be made for it as the one Alexander found among the spoils of Darius and set aside for the safekeeping of the works of the poet Homer. This book, my friend, is of authority for two reasons: first because it is very good, and second because it is said to have been written by a wise and witty king of Portugal. All the adventures at the Castle of Miraguarda are excellent and ingeniously contrived; the language is polished and clear, and the style suits the speaker with judgment and propriety. So then, if it seems good to you, Master Nicholas, I say let this and 'Amadis of Gaul' be exempted from the penalty of fire, and as for all the rest, let them perish without further question."
"No, my friend," said the barber, "for this that I have here is the famous 'Don Belianis.'"

"Well," said the curate, "that, and the second, third, and fourth parts, all stand in need of a little rhubarb to purge their excess of bile, and they must be cleared of all that business about the Castle of Fame and other greater affectations; to that end let them be allowed the overseas term, and as they mend, so shall mercy or justice be meted out to them. In the meantime, my friend, keep them at your house and let no one read them."

"With all my heart," said the barber; and not caring to tire himself with reading any more books of chivalry, he told the housekeeper to take all the big ones and throw them into the yard. It wasn't said to one dull or deaf, but to one who enjoyed burning them more than weaving the broadest and finest cloth she could make; and seizing about eight at a time, she flung them out of the window.
Carrying so many at once, she let one fall at the barber's feet, who picked it up, curious to know whose it was, and found it said, "History of the Famous Knight, Tirante el Blanco."

"God bless me!" said the curate with a shout. "'Tirante el Blanco' here! Hand it over, friend, for in it I think I have found a treasury of enjoyment and a mine of recreation. Here are Don Kyrieleison of Montalvan, a valiant knight, and his brother Thomas of Montalvan, and the knight Fonseca, with the battle the bold Tirante fought with the mastiff, and the witticisms of the damsel Placerdemivida, and the loves and wiles of the widow Reposada, and the empress in love with the squire Hipolito — in truth, my friend, by right of its style it is the best book in the world. Here knights eat and sleep, and die in their beds, and make their wills before dying, and a great deal more that you'll find nothing of in any of the other books. Nevertheless, I say that whoever wrote it, for deliberately composing such fooleries, deserves to be sent to the galleys for life. Take it home with you and read it, and you'll see what I'm saying is true."
"As you wish," said the barber; "but what shall we do with these little books that are left?"

"These must be, not chivalry, but poetry," said the curate; and opening one he saw it was Jorge de Montemayor's "Diana," and supposing all the others to be of the same sort, he said, "these don't deserve to be burnt like the others, for they neither do nor can do the harm the books of chivalry have done — they are books of entertainment that can hurt no one."

"Ah, señor!" said the niece, "your worship had better order these to be burnt as well as the others; for it would be no wonder if, after being cured of his chivalry disorder, my uncle, by reading these, took it into his head to turn shepherd and roam the woods and fields singing and piping — or, worse still, to turn poet, which they say is an incurable and infectious disease."

"The damsel is right," said the curate, "and it'll be just as well to remove this stumbling block and temptation from our friend's path. To begin, then, with Montemayor's 'Diana.' My opinion is that it shouldn't be burnt, but that it should be cleared of all that business about the sage Felicia and the magic water, and of almost all the longer pieces of verse; let it keep, and welcome, its prose and the honour of being the first of books of its kind."
"This next," said the barber, "is the 'Diana,' titled the 'Second Part, by the Salamancan,' and this other has the same title, and its author is Gil Polo."

"As for that of the Salamancan," replied the curate, "let it go to swell the number of the condemned in the yard, and let Gil Polo's be preserved as if it came from Apollo himself. But get on, my friend, and make haste, for it's getting late."
"This book," said the barber, opening another, "is the ten books of the 'Fortune of Love,' written by Antonio de Lofraso, a Sardinian poet."

"By the orders I have received," said the curate, "since Apollo has been Apollo, and the Muses have been Muses, and poets have been poets, no book so funny and absurd as this has ever been written; in its way it is the best and most singular of any of its species that has appeared so far, and whoever has not read it may be sure he has never read what is truly delightful. Give it here, friend, for I make more of having found it than if they had given me a cassock of Florentine stuff."
He set it aside with the greatest satisfaction, and the barber went on, "These next are 'The Shepherd of Iberia,' 'Nymphs of Henares,' and 'The Enlightenment of Jealousy.'"
"Then all we have to do," said the curate, "is hand them over to the secular arm of the housekeeper — and ask me not why, or we shall never have done."
"This next is the 'Pastor de Fílida.'"
"No Pastor that," said the curate, "but a highly polished courtier; let it be preserved as a precious jewel."
"This large one here," said the barber, "is called 'The Treasury of various Poems.'"

"If there weren't so many of them," said the curate, "they would be more relished. This book must be weeded and cleansed of certain vulgarities it has alongside its excellences; let it be preserved because the author is a friend of mine, and out of respect for the other, more heroic and loftier works he has written."
"This," continued the barber, "is the 'Cancionero' of Lopez de Maldonado."

"The author of that book, too," said the curate, "is a great friend of mine, and his verses from his own mouth are the admiration of all who hear them, for such is the sweetness of his voice that he enchants when he chants them. It gives rather too much space to its eclogues, but what is good has never yet been plentiful: let it be kept with those that have been set aside. But what book is that next to it?"
"The 'Galatea' of Miguel de Cervantes," said the barber.

"That Cervantes has been a great friend of mine for many years, and to my knowledge he has had more experience in reverses than in verses. His book has some good invention in it; it raises issues but brings nothing to a conclusion: we'll have to wait for the Second Part it promises — perhaps with revision it may win the full measure of grace now denied it; and in the meantime, señor friend, keep it shut up in your own quarters."

"Very good," said the barber; "and here come three together — the 'Araucana' of Don Alonso de Ercilla, the 'Austriada' of Juan Rufo, Justice of Cordova, and the 'Montserrate' of Christobal de Virués, the Valencian poet."

"These three books," said the curate, "are the best that have been written in Castilian in heroic verse, and they may compare with the most famous of Italy; let them be preserved as the richest treasures of poetry that Spain possesses."

The curate was tired and would not look into any more books, and so decided that, "contents uncertified," all the rest should be burnt; but just then the barber held open one called "The Tears of Angelica."

"I should have shed tears myself," said the curate when he heard the title, "had I ordered that book to be burnt, for its author was one of the famous poets of the world, not just of Spain, and was very happy in his translation of some of Ovid's fables."
